title: Identity and access management for AI agents
subtitle: I worked out, from real tenant evidence, how an AI employee legitimately answers, calls and acts inside Microsoft 365, with per-employee tokens minted server-side and never handed to a model.

stats.label: a pending client lives, for assistants that cache their client ID and never register again

lede: Auth and access plane: I wanted commercial AI assistants, including Microsoft Copilot Studio, to reach my private tool estate on my terms. I was not willing to run a server per vendor or hand out a secret per connection, so I decided that one OAuth 2.0 authorization server would issue every token and that a person would approve every client. I built that server in Python. It issues RS256-signed JWTs and supports the authorization-code grant with PKCE, client credentials and refresh tokens, revocation, and the published key set and metadata documents that MCP clients read first. Assistants register themselves as temporary clients and wait for a person. Interoperability was the hard part.
quote: Microsoft remains the permission authority for the digital employee, and my layer grants nothing the tenant has not.
evidence: OAuth 2.0 and identity architecture: one authorization server for every AI assistant, with PKCE, RS256 JWTs and a pending client lapsing after 30 days without a person's approval.
Microsoft 365, Graph and Entra integration: digital employees acting as themselves with per-employee Graph tokens minted on the server and never placed in a model's context.
Identity and least privilege for AI agents: Microsoft kept as the permission authority, typed refusals where no supported API exists, and one published key set trusted by three verifiers.
author: Corey James
